content: Ejada needs a supply chain management system to coordinate delivery of its information-technology products, consulting, and related services. Staff should be able to manage customer service, procurement, supplier and material selection, product development, manufacturing flow, physical distribution, outsourcing, and partnerships. The system should also help the company assess cost, productivity, assets, service, and quality performance across the supply chain.

The main reason is to have one coordinated view of everything we deliver, because our products, consulting work, and support services often depend on each other. Right now, delays or changes in one area can ripple into procurement, staffing, delivery dates, and customer commitments, so we want fewer handoff gaps and better control over cost and timing.
In day-to-day operations, the idea is that sales, procurement, project teams, and operations all work from the same information so they can track what was promised, what materials or resources are needed, what is in progress, and what has been delivered. That should make it easier to coordinate customer requests, supplier activity, production or implementation steps, and service follow-up without relying so much on manual checks and separate spreadsheets.

Beyond coordination, we want better control over cost, lead times, and resource use across the whole chain. We also want stronger visibility into supplier performance, inventory or material availability, and how efficiently we are using people, assets, and outsourced partners.
Another big objective is service quality and reliability, so we can spot delays, bottlenecks, and quality issues earlier. Ultimately, the system should help us make better decisions and improve productivity without losing sight of customer commitments.

In practice, I’d want the request to start with the business need, estimated cost, and expected delivery date, then route automatically to the right approvers based on the amount, risk, and type of commitment. Smaller routine requests could be approved by a department manager, while larger or strategic ones would need finance, procurement, and sometimes executive approval.
The decision should depend on budget availability, supplier or partner risk, contract terms, and whether the commitment affects a customer delivery or ongoing service. If it is tied to a live project or customer obligation, I would expect the project owner or service lead to be involved before anything is finalized.

Delegation should be allowed when the approver is unavailable, but only to someone with similar authority and knowledge of the work, not just anyone in the team. I would expect that to be temporary and traceable, so we can see who delegated it and for how long.
An override of the normal routing should be very limited, probably only for urgent business cases or exceptions, and usually restricted to senior management or the head of the function involved. Even then, we would still need a record of why the override happened and what approval was bypassed.

We usually treat products as the tangible or packaged deliverables, consulting as the advisory or implementation work, and services as the ongoing support, maintenance, or operational activity around them. The line gets blurry when a customer wants a bundle, so we would classify it based on the primary commercial purpose and how we plan to execute and invoice it.
If something could fit more than one, I’d want the system to allow mixed classification, but with one main owner area so there is no confusion about responsibility, costing, or delivery tracking.

If the work is split, the main owner should usually be the area that carries the biggest operational responsibility and customer-facing risk, not just the biggest invoice line. So if the consulting team is coordinating the whole delivery and the product is just one part of that package, consulting would own it, even if the product value is higher.
The main exception would be if a regulated or high-risk technical product is involved, where the product or engineering side must own it because of quality, compliance, or implementation control. In those cases, we would let the delivery risk and accountability matter more than the commercial split.

They need it most when they are coordinating new customer orders, checking material or supplier availability, moving work through procurement and delivery, and dealing with delays or changes in scope. It is also important when they are balancing multiple projects at once and need to see how one decision affects cost, timing, and service performance.
Day to day, I’d want the system to be simple to update, easy to search, and able to show the current status without forcing people to chase information in different places. It should give them clear alerts for exceptions, approvals, shortages, or overdue items, so they can focus on resolving issues instead of just tracking them.

For normal transaction entry, it should feel almost immediate, ideally a few seconds at most, so people do not get stuck waiting while they are trying to move work forward. For searches, status checks, and approvals, we would want the same kind of responsiveness because delays there quickly slow down the whole chain.
On accuracy, we need the system to be reliable enough that staff can trust stock, order, supplier, and delivery information when they act on it. I do not have a fixed percentage in mind yet, but it should minimize data mismatches and prevent incomplete or duplicate transactions.

Yes, some batch jobs would be fine overnight or end-of-day, especially routine updates, reconciliations, and reporting. Anything that affects operations for the next business day should be completed before staff start work, and if it misses that window, it should be flagged immediately because it can affect planning and customer commitments.
Different batches should be handled differently depending on urgency. A missed financial or inventory reconciliation can usually wait for a controlled rerun, but a missed shipment, procurement, or availability update should trigger an exception alert and maybe a manual workaround until it is corrected.

First, the business needs to be alerted clearly about what failed, what impact it has, and which orders, suppliers, or deliveries are affected. Then staff should have a way to switch to a manual workaround or an alternate supplier, so customer commitments are protected while the issue is being fixed.
After that, the system should help them prioritize recovery by showing what must be corrected first based on deadline, customer impact, and dependency.

We need very high availability during business hours, because even a short outage can delay orders, procurement, or delivery coordination. I do not have an exact uptime percentage agreed yet, but the acceptable downtime should be very low, and planned maintenance should be outside working hours wherever possible.
If something does go down, the system should recover quickly and not lose transaction data. For critical supply chain functions, we would expect continuity to be strong enough that users can resume work without re-entering a lot of information.

In practice, we should not lose completed transactions at all, and any in-progress work should be recoverable with minimal re-entry. If something was only partially entered at the time of the outage, it is acceptable to ask the user to finish it again, but we should avoid losing approved or submitted records.
The first items to restore would be anything that affects customer commitments, stock availability, procurement orders, deliveries, and payments. Those are the transactions that can create the most immediate business disruption if they are not brought back first.

It usually starts with a request from the business unit or project team, then internal review and approval based on budget and need. After that, procurement sources the supplier, issues the purchase order, receives the goods or service, and confirms that what was delivered matches what was ordered.
Once receipt is confirmed, finance can process the invoice and payment, with any exceptions held for investigation if there is a mismatch in quantity, price, or quality.

We need the system to show dependencies clearly before a decision is finalized, so managers can see what one project will delay, increase in cost, or put at risk. Priority should usually go to customer commitments, contractual deadlines, and strategic projects, but I would expect the system to make the tradeoff visible rather than deciding it automatically in most cases.
If one project consumes a shared supplier or delivery slot, the system should highlight the conflict and show the downstream impact on the other projects’ schedules and service levels. That way decision makers can compare options before approving the change.

We would definitely need managers, procurement users, operations or logistics staff, finance, and system administrators. Depending on how the business is organized, there may also be project leads or department heads who approve requests and monitor their own teams.
The exact role boundaries are not fully fixed yet, so we would want to define who can approve, who can edit transactions, and who can only view reports as part of the access setup.

Managers should be allowed to approve or reject requests, review performance, and override priorities only in exceptional cases. Procurement users should create and manage purchase requests and orders, but they should not be able to approve their own high-value transactions or alter finance records.
Operations staff should update receipt, distribution, and fulfillment information, while finance should handle invoices, payments, and cost records without changing procurement decisions. Administrators should manage users, roles, and system settings, but not be involved in business approvals unless there is a separate business role assigned to them.

They usually talk about purchase requests, purchase orders, receipts, invoices, and delivery status. For operations, they also use terms like assigned, in progress, pending approval, completed, delayed, and exception or rejected when something needs attention.
For reporting, they refer to cost, productivity, asset use, service level, quality, and supplier performance. Some teams also use project names, client names, and item or product codes as the main identifiers when discussing a record.

Yes, that happens a lot. Procurement might say purchase order while operations think of it as a supply request in progress, and finance may care more about invoice or payable status than the procurement wording.
The system should keep one official record and status behind the scenes, but it can display department-friendly labels where needed. When information is shared across teams, I would prefer it to show the standard term as well, so people can still understand the record without confusion.

In progress should be used when work has started and is moving normally, even if it is still waiting on supplier confirmation or internal processing. Delayed should be triggered when a promised date slips, a supplier misses a commitment, or an internal dependency blocks the work, and then the system should flag it for follow-up and rescheduling.
Exception should be used when there is a mismatch, missing document, quality issue, or some other nonstandard case that needs investigation, and rejected should mean the request or delivery cannot proceed as submitted. Completed should only be set once the item is fulfilled, verified, and closed out in the relevant workflow.

Yes, we would need rules for all of those cases. If supplier details are incomplete, the supplier should stay in a pending or incomplete state and not be used for critical purchasing until the missing information is filled in.
If certifications expire or ownership changes, the system should flag the supplier for review and revalidation before new orders are approved. Suspension should be possible when there is a serious quality, compliance, or performance issue, and then procurement should be blocked from selecting that supplier until someone lifts the suspension.

Managers should review the impact on cost, timeline, and service before approving anything that could affect another project. They should be able to compare the new commitment against existing commitments, available budget, supplier capacity, and any contractual or delivery conflicts.
If the change creates a risk to another project, the workflow should require an escalation or a second approval from the impacted area before finalizing it.

The supplier should first be put into a revalidation status so no new orders go through until the review is finished. Procurement would usually own the initial check, but compliance or legal should review certifications, ownership documents, and any risk concerns before approval.
If the change is minor, a standard review may be enough, but if ownership changed or a key certification expired, I’d expect manager approval before the supplier is reactivated. Once approved, the system should record the reason and the effective date so there is an audit trail.

Priority should usually go to the commitment with the earliest contractual deadline, highest customer impact, or strongest business value. If two items are still tied, then the one already approved and already in execution should generally keep its slot unless management decides otherwise.
The affected procurement or operations manager should be notified first, and if budget or service levels are at risk, finance or the project owner should be escalated to quickly.

It should escalate beyond the manager when the conflict could cause a missed customer deadline, a budget overrun, a contractual penalty, or a serious service impact. If the issue is only operational and can be solved by resequencing, then it can stay with the manager, but anything that changes cost or commitment terms should move up.
I would bring in finance first if the main risk is budget, the project or service owner first if delivery or service is at risk, and senior leadership if the conflict affects multiple departments or there is no clear tradeoff decision.

The system should flag an overrun as soon as actual progress starts slipping against the planned labor, material, or time baseline, or when forecasted completion moves beyond the committed date. If a cost threshold is being exceeded or a key resource is becoming unavailable, it should raise an early warning instead of waiting for the final variance.
Operationally, it should notify the responsible manager, show the affected customer commitment or project, and require a review of corrective actions like reallocation, resequencing, or approval for additional spend. If the forecast puts a customer commitment at risk, it should escalate immediately so someone can decide whether to recover the plan or renegotiate the commitment.

It should show the main cause of the issue, the options available, and the expected impact of each option on cost, time, and service. That would help managers decide whether to add resources, resequence work, substitute materials, or accept a controlled delay, instead of guessing.
Improving efficiency should not override a customer commitment when doing so would risk missing an agreed delivery date, breaching a contract, or degrading service for a key customer. In those cases, preserving the commitment comes first, even if it means a less efficient internal plan.

It should capture the full case history from the moment it’s opened until it’s closed, including who opened it, what the issue is, and every status change along the way. I’d expect stages like received, under review, waiting on action, being resolved, and closed, with timestamps and the responsible person or team for each step.
It should also keep the resolution details, any customer communication, and whether the outcome met the service commitment, so we can track recurring issues and service quality.

Yes, I’d expect a few exceptions. Anything tied to a same-day customer commitment, a downstream dependency, or a hard cutoff for shipment, production, or invoicing should be completed sooner than the normal overnight rule.
On the other hand, low-urgency batches like routine reporting, noncritical updates, or tasks with no immediate dependency can usually wait until the next business day or the next scheduled run.

The rule should be based on the nearest hard deadline and the amount of buffer time needed to protect the customer commitment or dependent process. If missing the deadline would stop shipment, production, or a service response, then it should be expedited immediately; if there is still some buffer, it can be scheduled for the next available run before the cutoff.
If the batch is important but not tied to a hard external commitment, then the system can keep it in the normal queue and just flag it as time-sensitive for review.

Yes, if the revalidation is due to a quality issue, late delivery trend, compliance concern, or a change in scope, the review should be stricter and may need additional approval from quality, procurement, or the business owner. If it’s a routine revalidation with no incidents, the normal procurement review may be enough.
If the supplier is critical to an active customer commitment or there are unresolved corrective actions, I’d expect management approval before reactivation. If there’s a regulatory or contractual risk, then the system should require whatever higher-level approval our policy calls for.

We’d want to bring over the active operational records first, like open customer cases, current purchase orders, supplier data, product and material masters, ongoing projects, and any live manufacturing or distribution work. Historical data should come across too, but mainly the records we need for reporting, audit, and trend analysis.
The parts that need special care are anything tied to commitments, inventory balances, financial history, and supplier status, because those have to be accurate on day one. I’d also treat open approvals, pending exceptions, and case history carefully so nothing gets lost or duplicated during the cutover.

The cutover rule should be that each of those records is frozen at a defined cutoff time, then reconciled against the source system before loading, with a unique reference carried over so the new system can detect duplicates. Anything that doesn’t match cleanly should be held in an exception queue and not go live until it’s reviewed and approved.
For balances and commitments, we’d want a final sign-off from the business owner and finance or operations, depending on the record type, before the data is marked as authoritative in the new system. That way we avoid gaps, double counting, or carrying forward the wrong status.

We should treat open approvals and pending exceptions as special-care items now, because if those are moved incorrectly they can block work or let something slip through without the right review. Case history should also be treated carefully, especially for active customers and suppliers, so the timeline and status are preserved.
If there are any other legacy records that aren’t clearly active or needed for audit, I’d leave those as undecided for the moment until we confirm whether they really need to be migrated.

The practical rule should be that a legacy record only gets migrated if it is needed for an active business process, a legal or audit requirement, or a current reporting need. If it doesn’t support one of those three, it should stay out of the new system.
That helps keep the new system clean and avoids loading old clutter that nobody will use.

Go-live should only happen after the migrated records pass reconciliation checks, duplicate checks, and spot validation by the business owners for the critical areas like commitments, inventory, supplier status, and open approvals. We should also confirm that any required reports and workflows are working against the migrated data before users start relying on it.
Anything with mismatched balances, unresolved exceptions, missing approval trails, or unclear ownership should stay in exception handling until a final business sign-off is completed. I’d also keep any disputed customer or supplier records out of normal use until someone formally approves the final state.

The main priority is keeping day-to-day operations stable, so anything that affects customer commitments, procurement, supplier performance, inventory, or manufacturing flow should get the fastest support. We should also prioritize issues that affect financial accuracy, service levels, and reporting, because those will quickly impact management decisions.
For future changes, I’d want a controlled process so migrated records can be corrected or enhanced without breaking audit history or creating new inconsistencies. Any change that touches active transactions, approvals, or supplier status should be reviewed carefully before it is applied.

A validation issue should block release if it affects a live transaction, changes a balance, breaks an approval path, or could cause us to ship, buy, bill, or report incorrectly on day one. It should also block release if we can’t trace the record back to a source or if the same issue is showing up across a meaningful group of records.
If the issue is cosmetic, limited to a non-critical field, or does not affect operations, then we can accept it with a documented follow-up after go-live. Even then, it should have an owner and a deadline so it doesn’t get lost.

The controlled process should require a logged change request, business owner approval, and whoever owns the affected area, like finance, procurement, or operations, to sign off before anything is changed. We should capture the reason for the change, the original value, the new value, the timestamp, and who approved and applied it so the audit trail stays complete.
For anything tied to active transactions, approvals, supplier status, or service continuity, the change should be tested in a safe way first or done during an agreed maintenance window if possible. If there’s any chance the change could interrupt work, it should be held until the impact is reviewed and the business confirms it is safe to proceed.

The authoritative status should be the one that reflects the current business reality and the most recent approved action, not just whatever the source system happened to store last. If the source data and migrated record disagree, we should prefer the status that is supported by the latest transaction, approval, or operational event, and if that still isn’t clear, the business owner has to decide.
For example, if a supplier shows as active in one place but there is a formal suspension or open issue, the suspension should win until it is resolved. We should not let a stale source status override a confirmed operational state in the new system.

If the change could interrupt an active transaction or alter an approval, supplier status, or customer service flow, it should normally wait for a maintenance window unless the business agrees it is urgent. If the impact is uncertain, or the change is more than a simple data correction, it should be tested first in a safe environment or on a non-production copy before we touch the live record.
It should be blocked until business review whenever the risk could affect commitments, billing, procurement, or continuity of service, or if there is no clear rollback plan. If we cannot explain exactly what will change and how we will recover if something goes wrong, then it should not go ahead.

Yes, anything that puts a customer commitment at risk should jump the queue, especially if it could delay delivery or change what we promised. The same goes for blocked procurement or a supplier issue that could stop materials, services, or outsourced work from flowing.
Issues that threaten financial accuracy, service levels, or management reporting should also be escalated immediately, even if they seem small at first, because they can affect decisions across the business. In those cases we would handle them with a fast triage and business owner involvement, rather than waiting in the normal support queue.

Essential for go-live would be the functions we need to run the business on day one, like customer service handling, procurement, supplier and material selection, core product and service flow, and the basic reporting we need to know what’s happening. Anything that supports those critical operations or keeps us compliant and visible to management should be in the first release.
We could defer more advanced optimization, deeper analytics, or nicer workflow refinements if the business can operate without them temporarily. The main test is whether postponing the function would slow down transactions, create manual work we can’t absorb, or put customers, suppliers, or reporting accuracy at risk.

Yes, if a function depends on incomplete data, an unavailable integration, or a failed approval path, we would rather keep it running manually than stop the whole operation, as long as staff can manage it safely. If the system output could be misleading or would create bad commitments, then it should degrade gracefully by limiting the function and making the restriction very clear to users.
We would pause the function entirely only when continuing would create wrong orders, wrong financials, or serious service disruption. In those cases, protecting customer service, procurement, and reporting continuity matters more than forcing the automated process to keep going.

I’d treat the current list as tentative for now. I don’t want to overcommit on functions we haven’t fully agreed with the business owners yet, especially around the finer points of manufacturing flow, outsourcing, and partnership handling.

For normal operational transactions, if the system is only briefly slow but the data is still accurate, we can usually keep going manually for a short time. If the response time starts causing missed approvals, delayed commitments, or users can’t trust what they are seeing, then the function should degrade rather than pretend everything is normal.
If the data itself may be wrong, incomplete, or duplicated, we should pause that transaction type until it is corrected, because bad records in orders, supplier commitments, or approvals are much harder to recover from later. We don’t have exact time thresholds decided yet, so I’d want to confirm those with the business and operations teams.

The responsible manager should be notified immediately as soon as the overrun is confirmed, not after the period closes. If a customer commitment, delivery date, or active project is at risk, then the escalation should move up to the next leadership level the same day, with enough detail to show impact, cause, and the recovery plan.
If the overrun is material enough to affect margin, service levels, or a major account, I would expect higher leadership and finance to be informed right away as well. The exact monetary thresholds are something we’d need to agree with management, but the principle is that anything threatening customer delivery or project success should escalate fast.

It can continue manually when the team can still complete the work accurately and there’s a clear way to record it later without losing traceability. That usually fits short outages, missing integrations, or temporary approval delays where staff can bridge the gap safely.
Even then, I would still want it stopped or limited if manual work would create too much backdating, duplicate entries, or inconsistent records, especially for commitments, costs, or reporting. If the workaround starts becoming a risk to control, then it’s better to restrict the function rather than let people push through it.

The department-specific label should be shown when the user is working in that department’s own context, because it matches their day-to-day language and makes the screens easier to use. But the standard term should also appear whenever the record crosses departments, is used in approvals, or feeds reporting, so people can tell they are looking at the same thing.
If there is any chance of confusion, I would prefer showing both labels together rather than hiding one. That is especially important for procurement, operations, and finance, where the same item can have slightly different names but still needs to reconcile cleanly.
